items.question: Our onboarding completion rate dropped from 62% to 48% in two weeks. How do you find out why?
items.answer: Segment before theorising: by platform, by acquisition channel, by cohort date, by step in the funnel. A cliff at one step and one platform points at a release; a gradual slide across all of them points at traffic mix. Look for someone who checks whether the metric definition or instrumentation changed before assuming user behaviour did.

items.question: Engineering says a feature you scoped will take three months, not three weeks. What do you do?
items.answer: Understand what drives the estimate before negotiating it. Separate the user problem from the proposed solution and ask what fraction of the value a smaller version captures. Bad answers push back on the estimate; good ones re-cut the scope or explicitly defer the feature and say what gets built instead.

items.question: How would you decide whether to build, buy, or partner for a payments feature?
items.answer: Is payments a differentiator or a cost centre for this company? Weigh time to market, compliance and PCI burden, margin on transaction fees, and switching cost later. Buy or partner when it is table stakes; build when the payment flow itself is the product experience.

items.question: Pick a product you admire and tell me one thing you would change, and how you would know it worked.
items.answer: Wants a specific change, not a wish list, tied to a user problem the candidate can articulate. The measurement half matters more: a named primary metric, a guardrail metric that must not regress, and a rough sense of how long it takes to read the result.

items.question: Your A/B test shows a 3% lift with a p-value of 0.04. Do you ship it?
items.answer: Not automatically. Check the sample size and duration, whether the test ran a full weekly cycle, how many variants and metrics were tested, and whether 3% clears the cost of maintaining the feature. Strong answers raise multiple comparisons and peeking without being asked.

items.question: How do you say no to a senior stakeholder's feature request?
items.answer: Acknowledge the underlying problem rather than the requested solution, show what the request would displace, and offer either a cheaper way to test the hypothesis or a date when it will be reconsidered. Look for someone who makes the trade-off visible instead of arguing about the feature.
